Model the end of the period as an intermediate catch event (a timer or wait) that is also a branch of the concurrent block. Connect the monitoring activity and the period-end event to a parallel gateway join, so that no branch ends on its own or bypasses the join. Continue from that join to the later step. Do not use an exclusive gateway to merge these branches.

When the description says an external device or party keeps sending back status or updates while the actor performs other work at the same time: Model the receipt of these ongoing updates as its own intermediate catch event on a branch that runs in parallel with the actor's other work, and do not omit it. Do not model it as a receive task, because the wait is for a recurring message rather than a unit of work. Join the branch back to the main flow when the work it supports completes.

Keep the handling of the remaining arrivals on their own branches, linked to the process so they do not block the continuation.

When the description says several activities are performed independently of each other and all of them must be completed before a later step can begin: Model a parallel gateway that splits the flow into one branch per independent activity, and a parallel gateway that joins those branches so the later step starts only after all of them finish. Do not leave the branches unsynchronized, and do not use an exclusive gateway for a join that requires every branch.

result.rule: Model performer information only when responsibility is stated. Prefer lanes for ordinary organizational responsibility.
Distinguish message tasks from message events: a task models performed work; an event models a message occurrence affecting flow.
Model every distinct activity, event, participant, decision, branch, loop, message and outcome stated in the description. Do not invent process facts.
Several unconditional outgoing flows from one activity can all proceed. Use a gateway when the description requires a decision or synchronization.
Use lanes to partition one process by a stated role, department, system or responsibility; lanes are not separate processes.
Use message events for directed participant communication, signal events for broadcasts, and timer events for stated dates, durations or cycles.

Model the subsequent step as its own task connected by a sequence flow, then join the branch to the next step of the process.

When the description says a participant records a fact, such as a problem found, a completed outcome, or a next due date, as an ordered step performed in that participant's own lane, and the step is part of the sequence of the process: Model each such recorded fact as a userTask in the lane of the participant who records it, placed in the stated order of the sequence, so that the recorded step is a performed task and not an event, a gateway, or an omitted step.

When the description states that an actor chooses one of two outcomes for an item they received, and the outcomes are stated as a choice the actor makes, not as a count or condition on other work: Model the choice as an exclusive gateway whose label is a question built from the decision the description states about that item. Label each outgoing flow with the outcome the description gives for that choice. Do not label the gateway with a condition on a different activity, such as a count of earlier updates or a count of recorded items, unless the description ties the choice to that condition.

When the description states that the process begins with a participant performing an action that the description itself presents as work carried out by that participant: Model the start as an unlabeled start event followed by a task that performs the described action (a user task when the participant works through a system). Do not put the action into the start event label, since that would drop the performed work from the flow.
